questions.answer: D: 4q (charge at Z is +4q).
steps: Let X be at 0, Y at d and Z at 2d, with k the Coulomb constant.
The force on +q at X from -q at Y is attractive, towards Y, of magnitude k q^2 / d^2.
For zero resultant, the force from the charge at Z must have magnitude k q Q / (4d^2) and point away from Y.
Setting k q Q / (4 d^2) = k q^2 / d^2 gives Q = 4q.
The charge at Z is +4q, which is option D.

The Earth's field points downwards.
A negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field direction.

questions.question: A spider of mass 3.00 x 10^-6 kg is pulled upwards by a strand of web carrying total charge magnitude 3.00 x 10^-7 C, in the Earth's field of 120 V m^-1 downwards. Determine the initial upward acceleration of the spider.

steps: Electric force on the strand F_E = |Q| E = 3.00 x 10^-7 x 120 = 3.60 x 10^-5 N, upwards.
Weight of spider W = m g = 3.00 x 10^-6 x 9.81 = 2.94 x 10^-5 N, downwards.
The initial upward acceleration is about 2.2 m s^-2.

questions.question: Determine the charge on 1 m^2 of the Earth's surface, assuming it is evenly distributed, that would produce a field of 120 V m^-1. Earth's radius is 6400 km.
questions.answer: Charge per square metre = 1.1 x 10^-9 C (equal to epsilon0 E).
steps: Field at the surface of a uniformly charged sphere: E = Q / (4 pi epsilon0 R^2) = sigma / epsilon0, where sigma is charge per unit area.
Therefore sigma = epsilon0 E = 8.85 x 10^-12 x 120.
sigma = 1.06 x 10^-9 C m^-2, so 1 m^2 carries about 1.1 x 10^-9 C.
The radius of the Earth cancels, because the charge per unit area is independent of the radius.

questions.question: An alpha particle of speed 1.74 x 10^7 m s^-1, mass 6.64 x 10^-27 kg, is reflected back through 180 degrees by a gold nucleus (atomic number 79). Calculate the maximum acceleration of the alpha particle at the point of minimum separation, with the nucleus at rest.
questions.answer: Maximum acceleration = 4.2 x 10^27 m s^-2.
steps: At closest approach the alpha particle is momentarily at rest, so all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy.
Charges: alpha q = 2e = 3.2 x 10^-19 C; gold nucleus Q = 79e = 1.26 x 10^-17 C.
Force at this separation F = k Q q / r^2 = KE / r = 1.01 x 10^-12 / 3.6 x 10^-14 = 27.8 N.

questions.question: An alpha particle with the same initial speed is deflected through a smaller angle. Explain whether its maximum acceleration would be the same as for the particle reflected back through 180 degrees.
questions.answer: No: the smaller deflection means a larger distance of closest approach, so the Coulomb force and hence the maximum acceleration are smaller.
steps: Maximum acceleration occurs at the point of closest approach, where the Coulomb force is largest.
A smaller deflection means the particle passes further from the nucleus, so its distance of closest approach is larger.
The Coulomb force is proportional to 1 / r^2, so a larger separation gives a smaller force.
Since a = F / m, the maximum acceleration is smaller than for the particle reflected through 180 degrees.

questions.question: The terminal velocity v of an oil droplet falling in air is measured with the plates uncharged, and upthrust is ignored. Show that the radius r is given by r = sqrt(9 eta v / (2 rho g)), where eta is the viscosity of air and rho is the density of oil. (The formula is not fully reproduced in the text extraction.)
questions.answer: r = sqrt(9 eta v / (2 rho g)).
steps: At terminal velocity the drag equals the weight: 6 pi eta r v = (4/3) pi r^3 rho g.
Cancel common factors: 6 eta v = (4/3) r^2 rho g.
Rearrange: r^2 = 9 eta v / (2 rho g).
Therefore r = sqrt(9 eta v / (2 rho g)).

questions.question: Millikan's value for the electron charge was 1.592 x 10^-19 C, versus the accepted 1.602 x 10^-19 C, due to an incorrect viscosity of air. Deduce whether the viscosity he used was too large or too small.
questions.answer: Too large: a larger viscosity gives a larger radius and mass, so the calculated charge is larger; Millikan's charge was too small, so his viscosity was too large.
steps: From Stokes law r is proportional to the square root of eta, so r^3 is proportional to eta^(3/2).
The drop mass m = (4/3) pi r^3 rho is proportional to eta^(3/2).
The charge from qE = mg is q = mg / E, so q is proportional to eta^(3/2).
Millikan's charge (1.592) is less than the accepted value (1.602), so his calculated mass was too small.
Therefore the viscosity he used was too large.

questions.question: The electric force on the ball in the uniform field between the strips is 1.9 x 10^-9 C charge at 1800 V over 2.0 cm. The ball (mass 0.18 g) accelerates at about 0.8 m s^-2. Deduce whether the electric force is the only force acting to accelerate the ball.
questions.answer: No: the electric force alone would give about 0.95 m s^-2, more than 0.8 m s^-2, so an opposing (resistive) force of about 2 x 10^-5 N must also act.
steps: Field between the strips E = V / d = 1800 / 0.020 = 9.0 x 10^4 V m^-1.
Electric force F_E = Q E = 1.9 x 10^-9 x 9.0 x 10^4 = 1.7 x 10^-4 N.
If F_E were the only horizontal force, a = F_E / m = 1.7 x 10^-4 / 1.8 x 10^-4 = 0.95 m s^-2.
The observed 0.8 m s^-2 needs a net force m a = 1.8 x 10^-4 x 0.83 = 1.5 x 10^-4 N.
The difference, 1.7 x 10^-4 - 1.5 x 10^-4 = 2 x 10^-5 N, must be an opposing force such as friction or air resistance.
So the electric force is not the only force acting on the ball.

questions.question: The shaded section of the model between X and Y corresponds to a drift tube in a linac. Give one similarity and two differences between how this section of the model works and how a linac drift tube works.
questions.answer: Similarity: the ball moves at constant speed through the section with no accelerating field, as a particle does inside a drift tube. Differences: the linac uses an alternating potential, whereas the model uses a fixed 1800 V / 0 V supply; the model ball is charged and discharged by contact with the strips, whereas in the linac particles are accelerated in the gaps between tubes.
steps: Similarity: inside the section the ball moves at constant speed because there is no accelerating field, as inside a drift tube.
Difference 1: a linac drift tube is supplied with an alternating (oscillating) potential, while the model uses a fixed 1800 V and 0 V supply.

Difference 2: in the model the ball is charged and discharged by contact with the strips, whereas in a linac the particles are accelerated across the gaps between the tubes by the field, without contact.

questions.question: In the model the drift tube lengths are constant. Explain why the lengths of the drift tubes in a linac are not constant.
questions.answer: The particles speed up along the linac, so each tube must be longer to keep the particle inside it for half a cycle of the alternating voltage.
steps: The alternating voltage must reverse each time the particle crosses a gap, so the particle must spend exactly half a period inside each drift tube.
As the particle gains energy its speed increases, so it covers more distance in the same time.
Each successive tube must therefore be longer, which is why the lengths are not constant.

questions.question: The graph shows how the field strength from a charged conducting sphere varies with distance. Which expression gives the electric potential at 0.5 m: A the area under the graph from 0 to 0.5 m; B the area under the graph from 0.5 m to infinity; C the gradient at 0.5 m; D E at 0.5 m divided by 0.5 m?
questions.answer: B: the area under the graph from 0.5 m to infinity.
steps: Potential is defined as the work done per unit charge bringing a charge from infinity, where V = 0.
V(r) = integral of E dr from r to infinity, which is the area under the E-r graph between r and infinity.
The gradient gives the field (not the potential), and E/r has no meaning for the potential.
So the potential at 0.5 m is the area from 0.5 m to infinity, option B.
